content: Lead exposure poses a significant health risk to children, leading to physical, cognitive, and neurobehavioral impairments. Numerous environmental sources of lead exist, prompting researchers to evaluate various household interventions aimed at mitigating or preventing lead exposure. This study is an updated review of prior research on the topic. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of household interventions in reducing lead exposure in children, with a focus on outcomes such as cognitive and neurobehavioral development, blood lead levels, and lead levels in household dust. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that assessed educational or environmental interventions, or a combination of both, targeting children from birth to 18 years of age. Eligible studies reported at least one standardized outcome measure. The review included 17 studies involving 3,282 children, with 16 RCTs and one quasi-RCT. Most of the studies were conducted in urban areas of North America, with one study each in Australia and China. The majority of the studies were conducted in low socioeconomic settings, and children under six years of age were the primary participants. The duration of interventions ranged from a single session to 24 months, with follow-up periods extending up to eight years. Three RCTs were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining studies had unclear or high risks of bias due to issues such as selection and attrition biases. Educational Interventions vs. No Intervention None of the studies in this category assessed cognitive or neurobehavioral outcomes, nor did they report adverse events. The studies focused on blood lead levels and household dust lead levels. The evidence suggested that educational interventions likely had no significant effect on reducing blood lead levels (mean difference [MD] –0.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] –0.13 to 0.07; moderate-certainty evidence) or floor dust lead levels (MD –0.07, 95% CI –0.37 to 0.24; moderate-certainty evidence). Environmental Interventions vs. No Intervention Dust Control One study in this category reported on cognitive and neurobehavioral outcomes, as well as adverse events. While the intervention group showed numerically better neurobehavioral outcomes, the differences were small, and the confidence interval included both beneficial and non-beneficial effects (e.g., mental development score: MD 0.1, 95% CI –2.1 to 2.4; low-certainty evidence). No adverse events related to the intervention were observed during an eight-year follow-up, although two adverse events occurred in the control group (very low-certainty evidence). Meta-analysis of blood lead levels found no significant effect of dust control interventions (MD –0.02, 95% CI –0.09 to 0.06; moderate-certainty evidence). Data on floor dust levels could not be pooled, but individual studies suggested no significant differences between intervention and control groups (very low-certainty evidence). Soil Abatement Two studies evaluated soil abatement interventions, focusing solely on blood lead levels. One study reported a small reduction in blood lead levels, while the other found no effect. The evidence was deemed insufficient to draw conclusions about the effectiveness of soil abatement (very low-certainty evidence). Combined Educational and Environmental Interventions vs. Standard Education Studies in this category reported on blood lead levels and dust lead levels but could not be pooled for meta-analysis due to substantial heterogeneity. The results were inconsistent, and the evidence was insufficient to determine whether combined interventions effectively reduce blood lead levels or floor dust lead levels (very low-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions The current evidence suggests that household educational interventions and environmental interventions, such as dust control measures, do not significantly reduce blood lead levels in children as a population health measure. The effects of environmental interventions on cognitive and neurobehavioral outcomes and adverse events remain uncertain. Further research is needed to identify the most effective strategies for reducing or preventing lead exposure. Future trials should focus on addressing multiple sources of lead exposure simultaneously, using empirical dust clearance levels as benchmarks. Additionally, it is crucial to conduct studies in lowand middle-income countries and among diverse socioeconomic groups in high-income countries to ensure broader applicability of the findings.
